The choice comes down to **which kind of file you edited**. There are five buckets:

| You changed | Run |
|---|---|
| Page content (a `.md` page in DA.live) | `sync_content` |
| Block JS/CSS in the storefront | `sync_storefront` |
| `mesh.json` / API Mesh config | `deploy_mesh` |
| A component credential (`.env`) | `update_project_config`, then restart the demo |
| A block you want pushed back to the shared library | `promote_block_to_library` |

Two things that trip people up:

2. **The hook only catches edits I make with Write/Edit.** If you edited files by hand or via a script, the hook never fired — call `sync_storefront` explicitly. It's safe to call even if unsure: it does nothing when there's nothing new to commit.

Also worth knowing: this all applies to EDS projects. Headless (Next.js) projects don't use content or storefront sync at all — you restart the dev server or redeploy instead.

said:
Here's the import path, no data touched.

## Call sequence

1. `find_datapacks` — see which packs exist
2. `get_datapack_import_target` — which Commerce instance this project implies
3. `list_datapack_import_scopes` — optional, only if you want a specific website/store view
4. `validate_datapack_import` — dry run, always
5. `start_datapack_import` with `confirm: true` — returns a job handle, not a result
6. `get_datapack_import_status` — poll until the outcome stops saying "watching"

Every write call needs all four of: `datapackName`, `version` (there's no "latest" — it must be named, e.g. `main`), `commerceInstance`, and at least one entry in `dataTypes` (omitting it fails; it doesn't mean "all").

## The three traps

1. **The start call is a receipt, not a result.** It returns as soon as the job is accepted; a big pack takes minutes. You must poll for the outcome. Also: an `unwatchable` outcome means the watch was lost, not that the import failed — the job may have finished fine.
2. **Never guess the Commerce instance.** It's deliberately not defaulted, because a wrong guess writes sample data into someone else's live demo. Use what `get_datapack_import_target` reports and confirm it; if it returns nothing, ask. Website/store view can be omitted safely (they inherit the project's scope), but send both or neither — half a pair is refused.
3. **Validate every time.** It's free and ungated, sends the exact same request as a real start, and stops. A `valid: false` answer is a verdict, not an error — read the reason instead of retrying.

## Worth knowing before you pick a pack

Some things the import can't check live on the Commerce instance itself: B2B data needs B2B enabled in the Admin; a non-default website/store view must already exist; customer segments aren't supported, so cart rules that reference them import but silently don't work. And after a successful import, the root category still has to be attached to the store by hand — until then the storefront looks empty.

When you're ready, tell me which project and I'll start with `find_datapacks` and confirm the target instance with you before anything writes.

The skill asks you to pick one of two paths up front:

**Workflow A — AEM Modernization Agent.** Pick this if you want the closest visual match and don't mind leaving the IDE. It runs in a browser at aemcoder.adobe.io, takes roughly 15–20 minutes per page, and commits finished blocks straight to the project's GitHub repo. You pull them back into the project afterward. It needs access provisioning (Slack request for Adobe employees, ~10 min) and a one-time GitHub connection per project. It refines its own output, so no local iteration loop.

**Workflow B — Playwright MCP.** Pick this if you'd rather stay in this chat, or don't have Mod Agent access. It's automated: I screenshot the reference at desktop and mobile widths, capture its structure, styles, and fonts, then author the blocks here. Faster to start, but the visual ceiling is lower, and matching happens through a local refinement loop capped at 3 rounds.

Either way, the same follow-up steps apply after the scrape: map product/listing pages to the Adobe commerce components, build the header/nav/footer, and swap the real site's data for demo-safe mock data.

## What to expect on fidelity

- Marketing pages: 80–90% match first pass, ~95% after refinement.
- Product pages: 60–75% first pass, 85–90% ceiling — the Adobe commerce components can only be customized so far.
- Animations and heavy interactivity: 50–70%; some won't translate.

For a demo audience, brand, layout, and major sections looking right is usually the bar that matters.

## My recommendation

If you have Mod Agent access (or can get it in ~10 minutes), use it — the quality gap is real. Playwright is the fallback when you want zero context-switching or access is a blocker.

said: Working on bodea… I'll load the commerce-block-mapper skill and walk through how it applies to your scraped product-page markup.

Here's how the mapping works, in plain terms.

## How scraped PDP markup gets mapped

The skill doesn't rebuild your reference page from scratch. It sorts the scraped markup into two buckets:

1. **The commerce core** — product gallery, title, price, variant pickers (size/color), quantity, add-to-cart. These all map to Adobe's `product-details` drop-in, a React component Adobe owns and ships. It gets *themed to look like your reference*, not rebuilt. (Same idea for other page types: listing pages → `product-list-page`, cart → `commerce-cart`, checkout → `commerce-checkout`.)

2. **Everything around the core** — related products, trust badges, brand messaging, distributor tables, custom CTAs. These become regular EDS blocks wrapped *around* the drop-in, where we have full control.

Then it extracts design tokens from your scrape — brand colors, fonts, spacing, border radius, button style — and applies them to the drop-in through its supported CSS variables. Fonts map onto the storefront's existing type scale rather than raw pixel sizes, so one adjustment retunes everything consistently.

## What's customizable vs. not

| You can change | You can't change |
|---|---|
| Colors, fonts, spacing, corner rounding (theming) | The drop-in's internal HTML structure |
| Content in the drop-in's named "slots" (e.g. a custom note under the price) | Areas where no slot exists |
| Everything surrounding the drop-in (custom blocks) | Replacing the drop-in with custom code |
| Reacting to its events (add-to-cart clicked, variant changed) | Its internal behavior |
| Display options via config | Features the config doesn't expose |

## The honest fidelity ceiling

First pass typically lands at 60–75% visual match. After 2–3 rounds of theme tuning, expect 85–90%. The last 10–15% is the drop-in's fixed structure — that gap doesn't close. The trade is worth it: the drop-in actually transacts with live catalog data, handles variants and accessibility, and keeps getting Adobe updates. A pixel-perfect static rebuild would do none of that.

One useful bonus: any PDP customization you make inherits on **every product URL** automatically — you customize one template, and the whole catalog picks it up.

If you point me at the scraped bundle, I can do the actual mapping — identify the commerce sections, pull the design tokens, and say block-by-block what goes where.

**The idea: keep the layout, swap the data.** The block structure, colors, fonts, spacing, and image sizes from the scrape all stay. Only the customer's real content gets replaced.

It handles two kinds of content differently:

- **Commerce sections** (product grids, prices, stock): nothing gets hard-coded. These sections fetch live from your demo's Commerce catalog, so the fix is making sure the demo backend has suitable products loaded. The real names and prices from the scrape simply never render.
- **Static sections** (testimonials, distributor lists, support contacts, logos): the real values are hard-coded in the block files, so those get edited directly — real quotes become generic placeholders, real distributors become "Distributor A / B", phone numbers become "Contact your account team". Counts stay the same so the visual rhythm doesn't change (12 testimonials stay 12).

A few other rules it follows:

- Real brand imagery is swapped for placeholder images at the same dimensions, so nothing shifts.
- Anything personal — reviewer names, "Welcome back, Jane" — is removed or made generic, not just renamed.
- No made-up trademarked brands as filler; neutral names or your prospect's brand only.
- A final sweep catches stragglers: links back to the original site, real product names in image alt text, brand mentions in code comments.

It ends with a local render and spot-check: no reference brand visible, no real part numbers, all images load, and the commerce sections still pull from the demo catalog.

Here's how the loop works, per the skill:

**Each round (max 3):**
1. **Screenshot the local demo** at desktop (1440px) and mobile (375px) widths, saved next to the reference shots.
2. **Compare section by section** — not pixel by pixel — and rank each difference: brand color/font/logo and missing or misordered sections are HIGH; spacing and type scale are MEDIUM; slight color shades, animations, and few-pixel offsets are LOW.
3. **Apply the smallest CSS/JS fix** for each HIGH/MEDIUM item. No restructuring blocks mid-loop — that belongs back in authoring.
4. **Decide:** if only LOW items remain, stop early. Otherwise go another round.

**Where it stops** — whichever comes first:
- All remaining differences are minor (LOW) — done, demo quality reached.
- Round 3 ends — hard cap, even if HIGH gaps remain. Then it reports honestly: what was fixed, what's accepted (e.g. animations EDS can't do), and what's still off with a proposed next step — usually a structural block rewrite, a commerce drop-in limitation to accept, or switching that page to the Mod Agent workflow.

The cap exists because the last 10% of pixel-matching burns hours for differences a demo audience won't notice. Brand, layout, and section completeness are the bar; a 4px offset isn't.

One check before running it: this loop is for Playwright-scraped references only. If bodea's reference came through the Mod Agent, refinement happens in its web console instead.

Want me to run round 1 now? I'd need the local dev server running and the reference domain folder name.

It's a single tool call: `promote_block_to_library`, with your project name, the block's folder name (its ID), a display title, a preview HTML snippet, and `confirm: true`. That one call does four things in order:

- **It's safe to re-run** while tuning the preview; only the doc page content changes on repeat calls.
- Registering makes the block *available* to authors — it doesn't place it on any page.

One heads-up from memory: the pre-commit hook blocks the auto-commit if the block folder lacks a `README.md`, so add one before registering or the block never reaches GitHub/live.
